title: Two Estranged Brothers Meet Again
overview: After twenty years apart, Jacob meets Esau, the brother he cheated, who greets him with tears and an embrace before the two go their separate ways.

parts.label: Jacob lines up his family (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Jacob puts the servant women and their children in front and Rachel and Joseph, his favorites, at the back where they would be safest. Bowing seven times while walking forward was a formal sign of deep respect, here a younger brother humbling himself before an older one.

parts.label: Esau runs to embrace him (vv. 4-7)
parts.note: Jacob had feared revenge ever since he took Esau's blessing (chapter 27), yet Esau runs to him, hugs him, and both weep. The text never says what changed Esau's heart, and readers differ on whether to credit God answering Jacob's prayer or Esau's own generosity.

parts.label: The gift and God's face (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: In that culture, accepting a gift from someone you had quarreled with was a sign the quarrel was over, so Jacob presses Esau to keep the animals he sent ahead. Saying Esau's welcoming face is like seeing God's face echoes the night before, when Jacob wrestled and said he had seen God face to face (32:30).

parts.label: The brothers part ways (vv. 12-17)
parts.note: Jacob declines to travel with Esau, citing his young children and nursing animals, and promises to follow him to Seir, Esau's home to the south. Instead he goes to Sukkoth, meaning "shelters," and interpreters disagree on whether this was sensible caution, polite custom, or Jacob slipping back into evasion.

parts.label: Settling near Shechem (vv. 18-20)
parts.note: Jacob arrives safely in Canaan, the land promised to his family, and buys a plot of ground there, though the value of the silver pieces is uncertain. He names his altar El Elohe Israel, meaning "God, the God of Israel," using the new name Israel he had just been given.

disagreement: Readers, Jewish and Christian alike, differ on whether Jacob's wariness and his failure to follow Esau to Seir show wisdom or his old habit of deception, which decides whether the chapter reads as a full reconciliation or a guarded truce.
think: When someone you once wronged welcomes you warmly, what makes it hard to trust that the welcome is real?
